passages.happening:
Isaac is old, and “his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see” (verse 1). He calls Esau, his older son. “My son.” “Here I am,” Esau replies.

“Look,” says Isaac, “I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death” (verse 2). He tells Esau to take his bow, hunt some game, and “prepare a tasty dish that I love and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
A blessing here is more than a kind wish. It is a father's solemn word over his son, spoken near the end of life. In this family it passed on the lead of the household and the promises God made to Abraham: the land, the many descendants, and blessing for the nations.

Isaac thinks he is dying. In fact he lives many more years. Genesis says he lived to 180 (35:28), and both his sons buried him (35:29). The hurry in this chapter rests on a fear, not a fact.

Notice what Isaac leaves out. Before the twins were born, God told Rebekah, ‘the older will serve the younger’ (25:23). Jacob has already bought Esau's birthright (25:29-34). Yet Isaac plans to bless Esau anyway, in private, with only his favorite son present. He does not call Jacob. He does not mention God's word.

And the plan turns on food. The word for ‘tasty dish’ comes up again and again in this chapter. Isaac ‘loved Esau’ because he ‘had a taste for wild game’ (25:28). The same appetite steers him now.
passages.later:
Jacob will bless his own sons before he dies (Genesis 49:1-28), and Moses will bless the tribes before his death (Deuteronomy 33:1).

Hebrews remembers this scene with surprising kindness: “By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future” (Hebrews 11:20). However flawed the moment, Isaac's words carried God's promise forward.
passages.asks: Isaac knew what God had said, and he planned around it. Ask whether there is something God has made clear to you that you are quietly working around. Then ask what appetite or favorite is steering you.

passages.happening:
Rebekah has been listening. When Esau goes out to hunt, she tells Jacob what she heard (verses 5-7). “Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you” (verse 8). He is to bring two young goats, and she will cook the dish Isaac loves, so that Jacob can take it in and be blessed (verses 9-10).

Jacob objects, but only to the risk. “Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned. What if my father touches me? Then I would be revealed to him as a deceiver, and I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing” (verses 11-12).

“Your curse be on me, my son,” says his mother. “Just obey my voice and go get them for me” (verse 13).

She cooks the meal. She dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes, and she puts the goatskins “on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck” (verse 16). Then she hands him the food and the bread (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
When Rebekah repeats Isaac's words to Jacob, she adds words he did not say: ‘in the presence of the LORD’ (verse 7). She understands the blessing as a holy act before God, not only a father's wish. That is why she thinks it is worth any risk.

Some readers think Rebekah acted out of faith in God's word to her before the twins were born, however wrongly she went about it. Others stress that she chose deceit and set her own son against his brother. The text does not tell us what was in her heart. It shows what she did.

Jacob does not say, ‘This is wrong.’ He says, ‘What if I am caught?’ His only worry is getting found out.

Rebekah's answer, ‘Your curse be on me’, is brave and also empty. No one can take another person's wrong on themselves just by saying so.

The plan is built on the senses of a blind old man. Isaac will taste the goat cooked like game. He will touch the goatskins and think they are Esau's hairy arms. He will smell Esau's clothes, with the smell of the field on them. Only one sense will tell him the truth: his hearing.
passages.later:
Paul writes, “Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return” (Galatians 6:7). This family will reap what it sows here.

Samuel later tells a king that obeying God matters more than any offering (1 Samuel 15:22). Rebekah's ‘obey my voice’ uses the same Hebrew words God used of Abraham's obedience in the chapter before (Genesis 26:5).
passages.asks: Jacob's only question was whether he would be caught. Ask whether that has ever been your only question. Then ask what it would mean to ask the other question first: is this right?

passages.t: ‘The voice is the voice of Jacob’
passages.happening:
Jacob goes in. “My father.” “Here I am!” Isaac answers. “Which one are you, my son?” (verse 18).

“I am Esau, your firstborn,” Jacob says (verse 19). Isaac asks how he found the game so quickly. “Because the LORD your God brought it to me,” Jacob replies (verse 20).

Isaac is not sure. He asks Jacob to come close, and he touches him. “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (verse 22). He does not recognize him, because of the hairy hands (verse 23). Again he asks, “Are you really my son Esau?” “I am,” Jacob says (verse 24).

Isaac eats and drinks. He asks for a kiss. When he smells the clothes, he blesses him: “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed” (verse 27). He prays for “the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth” (verse 28). “May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. May you be the master of your brothers” (verse 29). “May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Jacob lies to his blind father three times: ‘I am Esau’, ‘the LORD your God brought it to me’, and ‘I am’. The second lie is the worst. He uses God's name to cover his deceit. And notice the words ‘your God’. Jacob does not yet call the LORD his own.

Isaac's doubt is the saddest part. He hears his younger son's voice. He knows something is wrong. But he trusts his hands over his ears, because he wants to bless Esau. He believes what he wants to believe.

The kiss is a betrayal inside a family. The son kisses the father he is cheating.

The blessing is poetry. In Canaan's long dry summer, dew was the only water most crops received, so it was counted a gift of heaven. The last line echoes God's promise to Abraham: ‘I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you’ (12:3). The promise passes on, but it passes through a lie.
passages.later:
Jacob deceives his father with a goat and his brother's clothes. Years later his own sons will deceive him with a goat and Joseph's robe: “Then they took Joseph’s robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood” (Genesis 37:31). And on his wedding night Laban will deceive him, and Jacob will cry, “Why have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25).

Paul uses God's word about the twins to speak of God's choosing: “before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God’s plan of election might stand” (Romans 9:11).
passages.hard:
If God had said that the older would serve the younger, why does the blessing come through lies? Does God approve?

Genesis never says the deception was right, and it shows the cost in detail. Jacob loses his home for twenty years. He is deceived in turn. He lives in fear of his brother. Rebekah sends away the son she loves, and Genesis never tells of her seeing him again. Esau is left bitter. The habit of deceit reaches into the next generation.

God had already spoken (25:23). The scheme was not needed to make the promise come true. Like Sarah's plan with Hagar, it was an attempt to grab by cunning what God had promised to give.

Two things stand side by side in this chapter, and the text does not let either one cancel the other. God's purpose comes about. And every person who lied, schemed or played favorites did wrong, and their wrong bore real fruit. The note on Genesis 25:19-26 sets out how Christians understand God's choosing of Jacob, in the Reformed reading and the Arminian and Wesleyan reading. These notes do not settle it. On every reading, God's choice does not make Jacob's lie right, and Jacob's lie does not make God's choice wrong.

Later in Genesis Joseph says to his brothers, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (50:20). That does not excuse the brothers. It says their evil was not the last word. The same is true here.
passages.asks: Isaac trusted his hands over his ears because he wanted something to be true. Ask where you are believing what you want to believe. Then ask whether you have ever used God's name to cover something you knew was wrong.

passages.happening:
Jacob has only just left when Esau comes in from the hunt (verse 30). He brings his dish and says, “My father, sit up and eat of your son’s game, so that you may bless me” (verse 31).

“Who are you?” Isaac asks. “I am Esau, your firstborn son” (verse 32).

“Isaac began to tremble violently” (verse 33). He asks who it was that came, and says, “indeed, he will be blessed” (verse 33).

“When Esau heard his father’s words, he let out a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, ‘Bless me too, O my father!’” (verse 34).

Isaac answers, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing” (verse 35). Esau says, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me twice. He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing” (verse 36). “Haven’t you saved a blessing for me?” (verse 36).

Isaac says he has already made Jacob his master. “What is left that I can do for you, my son?” (verse 37). “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” Then Esau weeps aloud (verse 38).

Isaac speaks over him. His home will be “away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above” (verse 39). “You shall live by the sword and serve your brother. But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Do not hurry past Esau's cry. A grown man, a hunter, comes home to the father who loves him, and finds the one thing he came for is gone. He cries out ‘with a loud and bitter cry’. He asks three times. He weeps aloud. Genesis lets us hear all of it. Whatever Esau did with his birthright, this is a son's grief, and the Bible does not mock it.

Isaac trembles because he understands. He meant to bless one son, and God's word went to the other. Some readers think that in this moment Isaac sees that God's word to Rebekah has come true, and he stops fighting it.

Why could Isaac not take the blessing back? The text does not fully explain. It shows Isaac treating his spoken word as done: ‘he will be blessed’. Many readers think a father's solemn blessing, given ‘in the presence of the LORD’ (verse 7), was understood as a binding act, not a wish that could be withdrawn. Others think Isaac saw God's hand in what had happened and would not undo it. Genesis does not say which.

Esau's name for his brother is a bitter pun. ‘Jacob’ sounds like the Hebrew word for heel, and it can mean to trip someone up or cheat them. ‘Is he not rightly named?’

Isaac's word to Esau mirrors the blessing in reverse. Jacob was given the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth. Esau's home will be away from them. The small Hebrew word here can mean ‘of’ or ‘away from’. The King James Version reads it as a blessing like Jacob's. The BSB and most modern Bibles read ‘away from’, because the next verse describes a hard life. Both are possible readings of the Hebrew. Esau will live by the sword, but one day he will throw off his brother's yoke.
passages.later:
Isaac's last words to Esau look ahead to the history of Edom, Esau's people. David later ruled Edom: “all the Edomites were subject to David” (2 Samuel 8:14). In the days of King Jehoram, “Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king” (2 Kings 8:20).

Hebrews uses Esau as a warning: “See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears” (Hebrews 12:16-17).

Israel was still told, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).
passages.hard:
Hebrews 12:17 needs care. It says Esau ‘could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears’.

Readers take it in more than one way. Many hold that what Esau sought with tears was the blessing, and that he could find no way to undo what had been done or to change his father's mind. The Greek word for ‘repentance’ means a change of mind, and the American Standard Version reads ‘no place for a change of mind’. On this reading, Hebrews warns that some choices have results that cannot be taken back, however much we weep later. Others read the verse as saying that Esau's tears were sorrow for his loss, not sorrow for despising God's gift. Paul names that difference: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

What the verse does not say is that God turns away a person who is truly sorry and comes back to him. The rest of the Bible says the opposite. Jesus said, “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). Hebrews itself says, “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy” (Hebrews 4:16). And John writes, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). If you are afraid you have gone too far for God to take you back, this verse was not written to shut that door.

A word for anyone who grew up as the child a parent did not favor. Esau's cry, ‘Bless me too, O my father’, is in the Bible. God did not leave it out. If you know that cry, your hurt is real, and it was not your fault. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If the hurt is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: Esau's grief was real, and so was what he had thrown away. Ask whether there is something you once treated as worth nothing that you now long for. Then remember that God does not turn away anyone who comes back to him.

passages.t: Esau's grudge, and Jacob sent away
passages.happening:
“Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him” (verse 41). He says to himself, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob” (verse 41).

Rebekah hears of it. She tells Jacob, “Look, your brother Esau is consoling himself by plotting to kill you” (verse 42). “So now, my son, obey my voice and flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran” (verse 43). He is to stay there ‘for a while’, until Esau's anger cools and he forgets. “Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I lose both of you in one day?” (verse 45).

Then Rebekah says to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them, what good is my life?” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
Esau's grief turns into a grudge, and the grudge into a plan to kill. He will wait until his father dies and the days of mourning are over. But he means it. The verb for ‘kill’ is the one used when Cain killed Abel (4:8).

‘Why should I lose both of you in one day?’ Readers take it two ways. She may mean both sons: Jacob killed, and Esau put to death as a murderer (9:6). Or she may mean Jacob and Isaac, on the same day.

Rebekah thinks it will be ‘a while’. It will be twenty years (31:38, 41). Genesis never tells of her seeing Jacob again. Later only her burial is mentioned (49:31). She got what she wanted, and lost the son she loved.

Notice that she gives Isaac a different reason for sending Jacob away. She does not mention Esau's threat. She speaks of the Hittite wives that grieved them both (26:34-35). Rebekah still manages her husband. But this time her reason is also true, and the next chapter shows Isaac agreeing.

The chapter ends with the family scattered. One son is running, one is plotting murder, the mother is losing the son she favored, and the old father is blind and alone. That is where favorites and lies have led.
passages.later:
Obadiah, centuries later, speaks of the long bitterness between the two peoples: “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame” (Obadiah 1:10). A psalm remembers Edom's part when Jerusalem fell: “Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell” (Psalm 137:7).

But the brothers themselves meet again. “Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept” (Genesis 33:4). Years later they bury their father together (Genesis 35:29).

Paul warns, “Do not let the sun set upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26).
passages.asks: Esau nursed a grudge and called it comfort. Ask whether there is a grudge you are feeding. Then notice that this story does not end here: twenty years later the brothers embrace. Ask whether you believe God can do that in your family.
